title: Coaching Your Family Relationships
author: Tina Gosney
description: A podcast for parents seeking healthier connections with their adult children, addressing strained or distant relationships through family systems theory and practical guidance.

episodes.title: Failure to Launch: How to Help Your Young Adult Move Forward with Colin and Hayley from Not Therapy
episodes.summary: Guests Colin and Hayley from Not Therapy talk about supporting an unmotivated young adult living at home without enabling them, including executive functioning challenges and building independence.

episodes.title: How to Repair Your Relationship with Your Adult Child After Hurt or Conflict: Helpful Therapy Words, Part 3
episodes.summary: Tina covers two skills for reconnecting after conflict: repair and accountability. She explains how to acknowledge your impact without defensiveness or collapsing into guilt, and how apologies plus changed behavior rebuild trust over time.

episodes.title: How to Help Your Adult Child Feel Heard and Emotionally Safe: Helpful Therapy Words, Part 2
episodes.summary: Curiosity, attunement, and emotional safety in conversations with adult children, and how understanding their experience improves communication without requiring agreement.

episodes.title: How to Let Go of Control Without Losing Connection: Helpful Therapy Words, Part 1
episodes.summary: An introduction to differentiation and acceptance from Bowen Family Systems Theory, and how parents can stay grounded while respecting an adult child's autonomy.

episodes.title: Your Adult Child Calls You a Narcissist: What Are They Really Trying to Say?
episodes.summary: Tina clarifies the difference between clinical narcissism and emotional immaturity, and helps parents understand what their child may mean by the label and how to respond without defensiveness.

episodes.title: My Adult Child Says I Trigger Them: What Should I Do?
episodes.summary: How the nervous system responds to conflict, what Gottman Institute research says about emotional flooding, and practical ways to pause a conversation and come back calmer.

articles.question: How do you repair a relationship with your adult child after a fight?
articles.metaDescription: Coach Tina Gosney on repairing a strained relationship with an adult child: reach out first, own your impact without guilt, rebuild trust.
articles.intro: You repair a relationship with your adult child by taking the first step yourself, owning the impact you had without getting defensive or drowning in guilt, and then backing up your apology with consistent behavior over time. That's the approach Tina Gosney, host of Coaching Your Family Relationships, lays out in this episode. Her core warning is that waiting for things to blow over rarely works. Unresolved hurt doesn't fade. It usually turns into distance.

sections.heading: What happens after the argument matters as much as the argument
sections.body:
Most parents focus on the conversation that went wrong. Tina shifts the attention to what comes next. If a disagreement ends badly, if your adult child says you hurt them, or if you notice the calls getting shorter and less frequent, the days and weeks afterward are where the relationship is actually decided.

The tempting move is to give it time. Let everyone cool off. Wait for your child to come around. Tina explains that this waiting often reads to your adult child as indifference, and it lets the hurt settle into a pattern. The longer the silence, the more normal the distance becomes.

So the first practical step is simply this: don't wait for them to reach out first. If you value the relationship, you go first.

sections.heading: Repair is a set of intentional steps, not a mood
sections.body:
Tina defines repair precisely, and the definition is useful because it takes the vagueness out of "making things right." Repair means taking intentional steps to reconnect after conflict, hurt, or disconnection.

That can happen even when the underlying disagreement isn't resolved. You don't have to agree about the topic to repair the relationship around it. You can still think you were right about the thing and still acknowledge that the way it went hurt your child.

The host is clear that this is a skill, not a personality trait. Some people didn't grow up seeing repair modeled, and they treat every rupture as either permanent or something to paper over. Learning to name what happened and reach back toward the person is something you can practice.

quote.text: Repair means taking intentional steps to reconnect after conflict, hurt, or disconnection.
quote.speaker: Tina Gosney

sections.heading: Accountability without defensiveness or collapse
sections.body:
The second skill in the episode is accountability, and Tina describes two ways it commonly goes wrong. The first is defensiveness: explaining why you did what you did, pointing out what your child did wrong too, or minimizing the impact. Your child hears none of the apology and all of the defense.

The second failure is less obvious. It's collapsing into guilt, where the parent becomes so distressed about being a bad parent that the adult child ends up comforting them. The conversation that was supposed to be about your child's hurt becomes about your feelings.

Healthy accountability sits in between. You recognize the impact you had, you say so plainly, and you don't require your child to make you feel better about it. Tina notes that guilt and shame actively interfere with repair, because they pull the focus back onto you.

quote.text: Accountability means being willing to recognize the impact you had on your adult child without becoming defensive, collapsing into guilt, or deciding that you are a terrible parent.
quote.speaker: Tina Gosney

sections.heading: An apology opens the door; behavior keeps it open
sections.body:
The final piece is time. Tina explains that apologies matter, but they're the beginning of rebuilding trust, not the end. An adult child who has been hurt repeatedly will, reasonably, watch to see whether anything actually changes.

That means the apology has to be followed by different behavior, and that behavior has to be consistent. If you apologized for criticizing their choices, the test is what happens the next five times you're tempted to comment. One good conversation followed by a return to old patterns tends to make things worse than no apology at all.

The host frames this as good news. You don't have to find perfect words. You have to reach out, own your part, and then show up differently over and over. Trust is rebuilt in the repetition.

keyTakeaways: Don't wait for your adult child to reach out first; silence tends to become distance.
You can repair the relationship even when the original disagreement is still unresolved.
Accountability means naming your impact without defending yourself or making it about your guilt.
Guilt and shame get in the way of repair because they shift the focus back to the parent.
An apology starts rebuilding trust; consistent changed behavior over time is what finishes it.

faq.q: Should I apologize even if I think I was right?
faq.a: Tina's point is that repair and agreement are separate. You can hold your view on the issue and still acknowledge that the way the conversation went hurt your child.

faq.q: What if my adult child doesn't respond when I reach out?
faq.a: The episode focuses on what's in your control: reaching out, owning your part, and behaving consistently. Trust is rebuilt over time, so one unanswered message isn't the end of the process.

faq.q: How do I apologize without making it about my own guilt?
faq.a: Keep the focus on their experience. Recognize the impact, say it plainly, and resist the urge to explain yourself or seek reassurance that you're not a bad parent.
